description: We are TAKIMYILDIZ! Passionate about space, science, software, and AI, we aim to turn curiosity into creative solutions at NASA Space Apps Challenge. We welcome teammates interested in coding, UI/UX, data analysis, space science, or storytelling. No expertise required—just curiosity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn. Join us to share ideas, grow together, and build something meaningful!
summary:
Outpost Explorers is an interactive, browser-based 3D simulation that lets children aged 7–12 manage an outpost on the Moon or Mars. Players aim to complete a 12-phase mission while balancing energy, oxygen, food, and crew health.

Players allocate power to life support, plant growth, and scientific research. They also build shielding, send a rover to explore, and move astronauts into shelter during radiation alerts. Decisions produce visible changes: plants grow, solar panels fold, and the rover travels across the terrain. Lunar shadows and Martian dust storms create different planning challenges.

The project addresses the challenge by turning complex engineering trade-offs into understandable, hands-on choices. Saving electricity now may slow food production, while protecting astronauts can interrupt research. Scientific information drawn from NASA sources is clearly distinguished from simplified gameplay values.

Short guidance, interactive decisions, and opportunities to retry make learning accessible and engaging. By experiencing the consequences of their choices, children discover why careful resource management and planning are essential to sustaining human life beyond Earth.
details:
Outpost Explorers is a browser-based 3D educational game that helps children aged 7–12 understand the engineering trade-offs involved in maintaining a lunar or Martian outpost. Players must complete a 12-phase mission while keeping oxygen, food and crew health above zero.

How it works

Players begin by choosing the Moon or Mars. A short introduction leads them through power allocation for life support, growing lights and scientific research. They can then assign up to two crew actions per phase, including building shielding, harvesting crops, managing solar panels, sending a rover, entering shelter or requesting a forecast from Earth. Each action consumes resources, and players may skip jobs to conserve supplies.

After a choice, the decision panel closes so players can inspect the outpost. Selecting “Continue” opens the next decision; selecting “Run phase” applies resource consumption, crop growth and environmental effects. Plants visibly grow or shrink after harvesting, solar panels fold, shielding appears and the rover moves through the 3D environment.

The two destinations present different constraints. Lunar shadows interrupt solar generation, while Martian dust reduces sunlight and coats exposed panels. Communication with Earth is delayed on Mars. Solar-particle scenarios encourage players to weigh protection against productivity: shelter reduces harm but pauses scientific research.

Educational value and intended impact

The project teaches through consequences rather than long explanations. Reducing growing-light power saves energy but delays food production. Exploration consumes supplies that may be needed for survival. Shielding provides protection but costs energy and building materials.

Our intended impact is to make systems thinking, planning and resource management accessible to young learners. Failure produces an evacuation alert with an explanation, allowing players to retry with a different strategy. These educational benefits are design goals; formal testing with children has not yet been conducted.

Technology and creative approach

The prototype uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js and WebGL 2 for rendering. Procedural 3D geometry creates the buildings, terrain, astronauts, plants and rover. Players can rotate, zoom and inspect the scene. Node.js and esbuild support development and packaging; they are not required to play.

The game is packaged as a self-contained HTML file that can run locally without an account, external API connection or installation. Browser storage preserves progress. Motion, sound and graphics-detail controls offer flexibility for different preferences and devices.

Its central creative feature is the connection between guided decisions and visible changes in an explorable outpost. We prioritized short English instructions, clear resource costs, distinct planetary environments and opportunities to learn through repeated play.

Scientific grounding and transparency

NASA/SDO’s archived May 14, 2024 solar-flare report provides context for the solar-alert story. NASA information informs the communication-delay explanation. NASA CCMC DONKI was used as background research, and the Canadian Space Agency’s food-production toolkit informed the greenhouse concept.

These sources provide scientific context, not a live simulation feed. Resource values, crop-growth rates, hazard timing and health penalties are simplified educational rules. Solar-flare classification is not treated as a surface radiation-dose measurement. Sources and limitations are documented within the game and repository.

AI assistance and validation

OpenAI ChatGPT assisted with code, game logic, English text, documentation, testing and procedural 3D development. OpenAI image generation produced the labelled Mars panorama and artistic Earth texture. Google Gemini generated participant-provided visual references; those reference images are not included as game assets. No runtime AI service is used.

Automated checks cover simulation rules, guided interaction and obstacle-avoiding routes. Geometry and animation checks use a mocked renderer and do not establish real-device graphics performance. The prototype is an educational experience, not a mission-planning or safety tool.
